summary: Ethylmorphine (codethyline, dionine) is a semi-synthetic opioid closely related to codeine, used mainly as an antitussive in cough preparations and, less commonly, as a mild analgesic; it has also been used in ophthalmology (dionine) for ocular inflammation. It is a mu-opioid receptor agonist that suppresses the cough centre in the medulla and is partly metabolised to morphine by CYP2D6, so CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers are at higher risk of opioid toxicity and poor metabolisers of reduced effect. Like other opioids it can cause sedation, constipation, respiratory depression, and dependence, and it is markedly potentiated by alcohol and other CNS depressants. It is an opioid antitussive and is a controlled/scheduled drug in most jurisdictions. It is not FDA-approved in the United States; it is marketed in some European cough syrups (data from EU sources/monographs).

moa: Ethylmorphine is the 3-ethyl ether of morphine and acts as an agonist at opioid receptors, primarily the mu-opioid receptor in the central nervous system. Its antitussive effect results from direct depression of the cough centre in the medulla, raising the threshold for the cough reflex. As an opioid agonist it also produces analgesia, sedation, and, at higher doses, respiratory depression. Ethylmorphine is metabolised in the liver, in part by CYP2D6 to morphine (analogous to codeine), so much of its opioid effect in humans derives from this conversion; CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers form more morphine (greater toxicity risk) while poor metabolisers obtain less effect.

preg: Avoid where possible, particularly near term; opioids cross the placenta and can cause neonatal respiratory depression and, with chronic use, neonatal opioid withdrawal. Use only if the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.
lact: Avoid during breastfeeding; ethylmorphine and its morphine metabolite pass into breast milk and can cause sedation, poor feeding, and respiratory depression in the infant, a risk that is amplified in CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers.
renal: Use with caution and consider dose reduction in renal impairment, as opioid metabolites (including morphine glucuronides) can accumulate and prolong effects.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; altered metabolism may change the balance of parent drug and active morphine metabolite and increase sensitivity to CNS effects.

major: Other CNS depressants - alcohol, benzodiazepines, other opioids, sedatives, general anaesthetics - additive sedation and respiratory depression
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (current or within 14 days) - risk of severe, potentially fatal reactions
moderate: CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g., fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine, bupropion) - reduce conversion to morphine and may lower efficacy
Antimuscarinics and other constipating drugs - additive constipation/ileus risk
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - it markedly potentiates CNS and respiratory depression and overdose risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Detected on opioid toxicology screens; may raise plasma amylase/lipase (opioid effect on sphincter of Oddi).

missed: If you are taking it on a schedule and miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it. As it is often taken as needed for cough, only take a dose when needed. Never take a double dose.
overdose: Overdose causes the classic opioid toxidrome: pinpoint pupils, marked sedation progressing to coma, and respiratory depression, with hypotension, bradycardia, and risk of death; pulmonary aspiration and hypoxia may occur. The antidote is naloxone, titrated to restore adequate respiration, with repeated doses or an infusion as needed because the opioid effect (including the morphine metabolite) may outlast a single naloxone dose. Provide airway protection, ventilatory and circulatory support, and continued monitoring for re-sedation.
